B is correct. Mode = the value that appears most frequently. Tally: 2 appears 2 times; 3 appears 3 times; 4 appears 1 time; 5 appears 1 time; 7 appears 1 time. Mode = 3 (highest frequency). Trap: 2 = second-most frequent (not mode); never confuse mode (most frequent) with mean (average) or median (middle).

questions.stem: The mean of 10 numbers is 15. If one of the numbers (8) is replaced by 18, what is the new mean?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Original sum = 10×15 = 150. After replacing 8 with 18: new sum = 150 − 8 + 18 = 160. New mean = 160/10 = 16. Shortcut: mean increases by (18−8)/10 = 10/10 = 1. New mean = 15+1=16 ✓. Trap: 15 = no change (wrong — the sum DID change); 15.5 = adds 5 instead of 10 to sum.

questions.stem: The mean of five numbers 4, 7, x, 12, 9 is 8. Find x.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Sum = 5×8 = 40. 4+7+x+12+9=40. 32+x=40. x=8. Verify: 4+7+8+12+9=40; 40/5=8 ✓. Trap: 6 = if sum were 36 (wrong total); 7 = same as given 4 and 7 (wrong).

questions.stem: Find the MEDIAN of: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 (an even-numbered dataset).
questions.explanation: B is correct. The data is already sorted. n=6 (even). Median = average of (n/2)th and (n/2+1)th values = average of 3rd and 4th values = (8+10)/2 = 9. Trap: 8 = 3rd value only (not average); 10 = 4th value only; 11 = (10+12)/2 (used wrong pair).

questions.stem: Group A has 40 students with mean score 50. Group B has 60 students with mean score 60. What is the combined mean score?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Combined mean = (n₁×mean₁ + n₂×mean₂)/(n₁+n₂) = (40×50+60×60)/(40+60) = (2000+3600)/100 = 5600/100 = 56. KEY TRAP: arithmetic mean of 50 and 60 = 55 (wrong — this ignores unequal group sizes). The combined mean is closer to 60 because Group B is LARGER. Trap: 55 = unweighted average (wrong); 54 = wrong calculation.

questions.stem: The mode of a dataset is 7 and the median is 8. Using the empirical relationship (Mode = 3×Median − 2×Mean), find the approximate mean.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Empirical formula: Mode = 3×Median − 2×Mean. 7 = 3×8 − 2×Mean = 24 − 2×Mean. 2×Mean = 17. Mean = 8.5. Verify: 3×8−2×8.5=24−17=7 ✓. This formula (Karl Pearson's) works for moderately skewed distributions. Trap: 7.5 = arithmetic average of mode and median (wrong formula); 9.5 = (3×8−7)/2+1 (wrong manipulation).

questions.stem: 4 items are priced at Rs.10 each and 6 items at Rs.15 each. What is the weighted average price per item?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Weighted average = (4×10+6×15)/(4+6) = (40+90)/10 = 130/10 = Rs.13. TRAP: Simple average = (10+15)/2=12.50 (wrong — ignores that more items are priced at 15). The weighted mean is PULLED towards the larger quantity (6 items at 15 > 4 items at 10) → mean closer to 15 than to 10 ✓. Rs.13 is closer to 15 side ✓.

questions.stem: The mean of 5 numbers is 20. Each number is then multiplied by 3 and increased by 2. What is the new mean?
questions.explanation: B is correct. If every value is transformed as f(x)=3x+2, then the new mean = 3×old mean + 2 = 3×20+2 = 62. General rule: if all values undergo a linear transformation (ax+b), the mean transforms as a×mean+b. New mean=3×20+2=62. Verify: if 5 numbers have mean 20 (sum=100), after ×3 sum=300 (mean=60), after +2 each: sum=300+5×2=310; mean=310/5=62 ✓. Trap: 60 = forgot the +2 per number; 65 = added 5 (total added as single value rather than per number).
